name: Orbital rim implants

lead: Orbital rim implants are synthetic implants placed on the bony rim under the eye to reduce hollowing and support the lower lid, giving a smoother, more supported under-eye. They are sometimes combined with cheek (malar) implants. Hardmaxxing forums discuss them as a durable alternative to filler.

A silicone, porous polyethylene or similar implant, standard or custom-made from CT scans, is placed under the periosteum of the rim and secured, adding projection to the bony support. Published data on cosmetic use are limited, and much of the satisfaction data comes from malar implants.

paras: It is a surgical procedure done under anaesthesia by a facial surgeon, with recovery of several weeks. Forum discussion centres on standard versus custom designs and on pairing with cheek implants.

Reported complications include lower eyelid malposition, infection, contour irregularities and implant extrusion, and rarely nerve injury or sinus fistula. It is major facial surgery, so people with active infection or unrealistic expectations are typically advised against it.

angle.text: Implants along the lower orbital rim build bony support under the eye and smooth hollows and tear troughs, a change you can see once healed. It is promoted as more durable than fillers. Published data on cosmetic use is thin.

lead: Infraorbital or orbital rim implants are alloplastic (synthetic) devices placed along the lower orbital rim to add bony support under the eye. People use them to make the eye area look less hollow and less prominent: by moving the rim forward, the implant is intended to soften under-eye hollows and tear trough shadows, correct a negative orbital vector (where the front of the eyeball projects beyond the cheek support), and create a smoother line from lower eyelid to cheek [1]. Grokipedia describes them as typically made of medical-grade silicone and presents them as a more durable alternative to fillers or fat grafting, which can resorb in this area [1].

The implants may be standard, prefabricated pieces aimed at the tear trough region, or custom pieces designed from CT data and often extending into the malar (cheekbone) area. They are sometimes combined with midface lifts, lateral canthopexy or lower blepharoplasty to optimise lower eyelid position and the lid-cheek transition [1][2].

Published evidence on the cosmetic use is limited to case series and reports. A 2003 case series of 41 patients described hand-carved ePTFE orbital rim implants used with midface lifting, with complications limited to implant palpability, one removal for infection tied to recurrent squamous cell carcinoma, and one revisional canthoplasty [3]. In looksmaxxing forums the implants are discussed, often alongside malar implants, as a hardmaxxing option for eye-area and midface support, with debate over what they can and cannot change, including a thread arguing they move the bone forward rather than adding support in the soft tissue under the eye [4].

paras: The infraorbital rim is the lower edge of the bony eye socket. Wikipedia describes the orbital margin's lower border as formed by the maxilla and the zygomatic bone, with the infraorbital nerve emerging through a foramen just below it [5]. The rim supports the lower eyelid and defines where the lid meets the cheek, so its position relative to the front of the eyeball shapes how hollow or prominent the eye looks [1].

An orbital rim implant is a shaped piece of synthetic material fixed on the surface of that bone, beneath the periosteum, so that the rim projects further forward. Grokipedia presents the goals as reversing a negative orbital vector, reducing scleral show (visible white below the iris), smoothing the lid-cheek junction and giving more lasting structural support than fillers or fat grafting [1]. Because the implant sits on the bony edge, some forum posters argue that it does not itself fill the soft area beneath the eye, and that a 'saddle' extension, fat grafting or filler is what adds volume there [4].

According to Grokipedia, solid silicone is inert and encapsulated by scar tissue, which makes it easier to remove at revision, while porous polyethylene has pores of about 100-150 micrometres that allow tissue ingrowth and is typically screw-fixed; PEEK and ePTFE are used less often [1]. Wikipedia's cheek augmentation article lists solid silicone, Medpor (high-density porous polyethylene) and ePTFE as the common cheek implant materials; Medpor and ePTFE integrate better with tissue than silicone, though Medpor's ingrowth can make revision harder [6].

Standard implants are prefabricated for milder cases focused on the tear trough, with extended versions reaching into the cheek. Custom implants are built from a patient's CT data and may extend into the cheek, and combined infraorbital-malar designs address both areas in one device [1]. Terminology varies: orbital rim implant, infraorbital rim implant and tear trough implant are used interchangeably in some literature, although tear trough implant can refer to the medial part of the rim [1][7].

Grokipedia lists indications including congenital midface hypoplasia, age-related skeletal loss, tear trough deformity, infraorbital rim recession, scleral show and post-blepharoplasty lid malposition, particularly where the eye projects beyond the cheek [1]. It attributes tear trough deformity to a mix of bone resorption, fat atrophy, ligament laxity, skin thinning and midface descent [1].

Sagittal measurements cited by Grokipedia place the rim about 12 mm behind the front of the globe in typical Western orbits, slightly less in East Asian orbits, with the rim about 2-3 mm behind the cornea in youthful faces and the infraorbital nerve roughly 7-8 mm below the rim [1]. Looksmaxxing posts about a negative orbital vector use similar language [8]. Posters also point to differences between people: one thread argues that East Asian faces often have projecting infraorbital rims yet shallow-looking eyes because of limited supraorbital prominence [9].

The implant is described as placed in a pocket beneath the periosteum through a conjunctival, intraoral or lower-eyelid approach, protecting the infraorbital nerve with a notch in the implant and secured with sutures or small screws [1]. Wikipedia notes that cheek implant surgery is usually done under sedation or general anaesthesia, takes one to two hours, and that intraoral incisions carry a higher infection risk than external ones, which can leave a visible scar [6]. Grokipedia reports a mean projection enhancement of about 4.6 mm in porous polyethylene series [1].

Swelling and bruising are reported to improve over one to three weeks, with activity restrictions around two weeks, numbness in the cheek and upper lip lasting several weeks, and most people returning to light work within about a week [1]. Planning for custom pieces commonly uses three-dimensional CT [1].

sections.h: Relationship to blepharoplasty and midface lifts
paras: Lower blepharoplasty reshapes the eyelid-cheek contour; Wikipedia describes transcutaneous and transconjunctival approaches, notes that canthopexy or canthoplasty may be added to stabilise the lateral eyelid, and describes fat repositioning along the infraorbital rim to address tear trough deformities [2]. A review of transconjunctival fat repositioning says traditional removal of herniated fat can leave a sunken or hollow lower lid, particularly with a tear-trough deformity, and that repositioning fat into the nasojugal fold may prevent this.

Orbital rim implants also appear in reconstructive eyelid and midface work. A review of treatments for post-blepharoplasty lower eyelid retraction describes using a hand-carved ePTFE implant held with microscrews to provide volume at the orbital rim and to anchor lifted cheek soft tissue, and a 2015 review of the transpalpebral midface lift places that operation within an evolution toward more vertical vectors of lift. A randomised controlled trial published in 2021 studied subperiosteal midface lift combined with lipofilling in patients with negative lower eyelid vectors.

A 2003 case series of 41 consecutive patients treated with hand-carved ePTFE orbital rim implants during transconjunctival midface surgery, with at least six months of follow-up, reported that significant complications were limited: two cases of implant palpability (one needing modification), one removal because of skin breakdown and infection tied to recurrent squamous cell carcinoma, and one revisional lateral canthoplasty for symmetry [3]. Grokipedia reports a 10-patient series with about three years of follow-up showing stable results without infection or nerve damage, and notes that its satisfaction figures (97.7% in 129 transfeminine patients, 85% rating results excellent in a Silastic malar series) come from malar rather than orbital rim implants [1].

Reported complications in general include lower eyelid malposition, infection, contour irregularities, asymmetry and extrusion, with rarer nerve injury, lacrimal sac penetration and sinus fistula [1][6]. A 2011 case report described orbital emphysema with painful limited eye movement and proptosis in a man with Crouzon syndrome after removal of bilateral malar and orbital rim implants, attributed to hydrogen peroxide entering through a suspected perforation of the orbital septum; it settled with conservative management [10].

No controlled clinical studies on cosmetic infraorbital rim implants were found. Published reports are case series and case reports: a 41-patient retrospective series of ePTFE orbital rim implants with midface lifting (2003) and a case report of orbital emphysema after implant removal (2011) [3][10]. Related work includes a 1999 CT study on a cadaver skull measuring orbital volume after lateral orbital rim implant placement for thyroid eye disease, and a registered post-market follow-up of customised PEEK implants (n=99), which concerns cranial and craniofacial indications [11][12].

Looksmax.org threads cover surgeon recommendations including options in Europe, questions about whether rim implants alone can lift the lower eyelids, whether implants made from the patient's own bone offer an alternative, and how rim implants differ from tear trough fillers, malar implants and cheek fillers [13][14][15][7][16][17]. Other posts ask whether the surgery makes enough of a difference or whether it is overrated, and one thread explains negative orbital vector in relation to the implants [18][8].

A thread titled 'orbital rim implants are a psl meme' argues that they mainly make eyes look more deep-set, that fillers add volume under the eye, and that small changes in orbital vector matter little to attraction; a reply says it is not a meme if it makes you look better [9]. Users compare infraorbital rim and malar implants, with some stating that off-the-shelf malar implants add too much lower-face volume and that custom implants are needed for men. Others post results and question whether implants altered the cheek contour.

lore.intro: Orbital rim and malar implants are discussed on looksmax.org as hardmaxxing options for under-eye and midface support, often framed around a negative orbital vector, and members debate how large the change is [18][9].
